On Persistence and Stability of some Biological Systems with Cross Diffusion

E. Ahmed    A. S. Hegazi    A. S. Elgazzar Affiliation: Mathematics Department, Faculty of Science35516 Mansoura, Egypt Affiliation: Mathematics Department, Faculty of ScienceAl-Ain, P. O. Box 17551, UAE Affiliation: Mathematics Department, Faculty of Science - Al-JoufKing Soad University, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia Affiliation: Mathematics Department, Faculty of Education45111 El-Arish, Egypt
Abstract

The concept of cross diffusion is applied to some biological systems. The conditions for persistence and Turing instability in the presence of cross diffusion are derived. Many examples including: predator-prey, epidemics (with and without delay), hawk-dove-retaliate and prisoner’s dilemma games are given.

1 Introduction

Cross diffusion is the diffusion of one type of species due to the presence of another [Okubo 1980, Chattopadhyay and Chatterjee 2001]. This phenomena is abundant in nature e.g. predator-prey systems where the predator diffuses towards the regions where the prey is more abundant. On the other hand, the prey tries to avoid predators by diffusing away from them. Another area of application is in epidemics where susceptible individuals try to avoid infected individuals.

Our aim is to generalize some biological systems to the case of the presence of cross diffusion. We study the persistence and Turing instability of the generalized models. Several examples are given e.g. predator-prey system, epidemic model, hawk-dove-retaliate game and prisoner’s dilemma game.

The paper is organized as follows: In section 2 the conditions for Turing instability in the presence of cross diffusion are derived then applied to a predator-prey system. Necessary conditions for persistence of a predator prey system in the presence of cross diffusion are derived. In section 3, cross diffusion is introduced in an epidemic model. Its effect on wave solution with and without delay is derived. In section 4, the effect of cross diffusion on evolutionarily stable strategy is studied. Hawk-dove-retaliate game is given as an example. Cross diffusion is applied to the dynamics of learning in multiagent systems in section 5. Some conclusions are summarized in section 6.

2 Cross diffusion in a predator-prey model

Cross diffusion is expected to be relevant to predator-prey systems where the predator diffuses towards the regions where the prey is more abundant. On the other hand, the prey tries to avoid predators by diffusing away from them. Cross diffusion term expresses the population flux of one species due to the presence of another species. The value of the cross diffusion may be positive, negative or zero.

Positive cross diffusion means that one type of species tends to move in the direction of lower density of the other type and vice versa. Hence the cross diffusion term is positive for the prey and negative for the predator. Generalizing Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model (with prey saturation) to include cross diffusion, one gets

∂u1∂t=u1​(α1−β1​u1−u2)+D1​∂2u1∂x2+∂∂x​(D12′​(u1)​∂u2∂x),∂u2∂t=u2​(−α2+u1)+D2​∂2u2∂x2−∂∂x​(D21′​(u2)​∂u1∂x),\begin{array}[]{l}\frac{\partial u_{1}}{\partial t}=u_{1}(\alpha_{1}-\beta_{1}u_{1}-u_{2})+D_{1}\frac{\partial^{2}u_{1}}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(D_{12}^{\prime}(u_{1})\frac{\partial u_{2}}{\partial x}),\\ \frac{\partial u_{2}}{\partial t}=u_{2}(-\alpha_{2}+u_{1})+D_{2}\frac{\partial^{2}u_{2}}{\partial x^{2}}-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(D_{21}^{\prime}(u_{2})\frac{\partial u_{1}}{\partial x}),\end{array} (1)

where D12′​(u1)D_{12}^{\prime}(u_{1}) is the density dependent diffusion coefficient of cross diffusion such that D12′​(u1)→0​a​s​u1→0.D_{12}^{\prime}(u_{1})\rightarrow 0\;as\;u_{1}\rightarrow 0.\;Following Chattopadhyay and Chatterjee [Chattopadhyay and Chatterjee 2001] we assume that

D12′=D12​u1/(ϵ+u1)≈D12​(1−ϵ/u1+…),D_{12}^{\prime}=D_{12}u_{1}/(\epsilon+u_{1})\approx D_{12}(1-\epsilon/u_{1}+...),

where ϵ\epsilon is very small hence

D12′≈D12​∀u1>>ϵ.D_{12}^{\prime}\approx D_{12}\;\;\forall u_{1}>>\epsilon.

Similarly for D21D_{21} thus we get

∂u1∂t=u1​(α1−β1​u1−u2)+D1​∂2u1∂x2+D12​∂2u2∂x2,∂u2∂t=u2​(−α2+u1)+D2​∂2u2∂x2−D21​∂2u1∂x2,\begin{array}[]{l}\frac{\partial u_{1}}{\partial t}=u_{1}(\alpha_{1}-\beta_{1}u_{1}-u_{2})+D_{1}\frac{\partial^{2}u_{1}}{\partial x^{2}}+D_{12}\frac{\partial^{2}u_{2}}{\partial x^{2}},\\ \frac{\partial u_{2}}{\partial t}=u_{2}(-\alpha_{2}+u_{1})+D_{2}\frac{\partial^{2}u_{2}}{\partial x^{2}}-D_{21}\frac{\partial^{2}u_{1}}{\partial x^{2}},\end{array} (2)

We have used −D21-D_{21} since predators move to regions with higher prey density. The value α1\alpha_{1} is the net growth rate of the prey population in the absence of predators, while α2\alpha_{2} is the net death rate of predators due to the absence of prey. The term β1​u1\beta_{1}u_{1} corresponds to the competition within the prey species.

The existence of solutions of systems similar to (2) has been studied in [Chen et al 2003 and Le 2003].

This system has a unique homogeneous coexistence solution

u1∗=α2,u2∗=α1−α2​β1,α1−α2​β1>0.u_{1}^{*}=\alpha_{2},\;\;\;u_{2}^{*}=\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\beta_{1},\;\;\;\;\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\beta_{1}>0.\;\; (3)

Now the persistence of the system (2) is discussed:

Definition 1: A partial differential equation

F⁡(t,x,u⁡(t,x),∂u/∂t,∂u/∂x,…)=0,F(t,x,u(t,x),\partial u/\partial t,\partial u/\partial x,...)=0,

defined on a spatial domain Ω\Omega is persistent in the context of zero Dirichlet boundary conditions if there exist a region V={u: 0<u<w}V=\{u:\;0<u<w\} in Ω\Omega such that all solutions with nontrivial, nonnegative initial conditions are attracted to VV.

Equivalently the boundary of the positive cone in the space where the solutions exist act as a repeller.

Persistence [Hofbauer and Sigmund 1998] is an important concept in population biology since it means that a certain species will continue to exist. The work of Cantrell et al [Cantrell et al 1993] is basic in finding sufficient conditions for persistence in some partial differential equations without cross diffusion. Therefore we will use it to derive the necessary conditions for persistence of the system (2). Here zero Dirichlit boundary conditions are assumed:

ui=0​at​x=0,x=L.u_{i}=0\;\mathrm{at}\;x=0,\;x=L.

3 Cross diffusion in epidemics

In this section, we will study an epidemic model where the population is classified into susceptible (S), and infected and infective (I), according to the health of each individual. The transition between the two states occurs according to the following rules:

  1. Susceptible individual having at least one infected nearest neighbor is infected in the next time step.

  2. Infected individuals are recovered and become susceptible with a rate λ\lambda.

Cross diffusion will be included, where S-individuals diffuse away from I-individuals. This system will be studied both without and with delay. In the first case we have

∂S∂t=−S​I,∂I∂t=S​I−λ​I−D​∂2S∂x2,\begin{array}[]{l}\frac{\partial S}{\partial t}=-SI,\\ \frac{\partial I}{\partial t}=SI-\lambda I-D\frac{\partial^{2}S}{\partial x^{2}},\end{array} (14)

where both λ\lambda and DD are nonnegative constants.

Here we consider that only susceptibles are capable of diffusing. This corresponds to the case where the disease has symptoms hence susceptibles try to avoid infectives.

Studying the wave solution of Eq. (14)

S=S⁡(z),I=I⁡(z),z=x−c​t,S=S(z),\;I=I(z),\;z=x-ct,

with the boundary conditions

S⁡(∞)≃1,0≤S⁡(−∞)≤1,I⁡(∞)=I⁡(−∞)≃0,S(\infty)\simeq 1,0\leq S(-\infty)\leq 1,\;I(\infty)=I(-\infty)\simeq 0, (15)

one gets

I=c​S′S,−c​I′=−D​S′′−λ​I+S​I,S′=d​Sd​z,I′=d​Id​z.I=c\frac{S^{\prime}}{S},\;-cI^{\prime}=-DS^{\prime\prime}-\lambda I+SI,\;\;S^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}z},\;I^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}z}.

Substituting from the first equation and integrating the second one, we get

F−c​I=−D​S​Ic−λ​c​ln⁡S+c​S.F-cI=-D\frac{SI}{c}-\lambda c\ln S+cS.

To determine the constant (FF), consider z→∞z\rightarrow\infty i.e. the past then Eq. (15) implies that F=cF=c. Now consider the future z→−∞z\rightarrow-\infty, and let S⁡(t=∞)=σS(t=\infty)=\sigma, then the fraction of survivors σ\sigma is given by the transcendental equation as follows:

1−σln⁡(σ)=λ,\frac{1-\sigma}{\ln(\sigma)}=\lambda, (16)

which is identical to an equation obtained by Murray [Murray 1993] in another context.

It is straightforward to see that the homogeneous solution (S=1,I=0)(S=1,\;I=0) is asymptotically stable if

λ<1,c≥D.\lambda<1,\;\ c\geq\sqrt{D}. (17)

Introducing delay, the system (14) becomes

∂S∂t=−S​I,∂I∂t=S⁡(x,t−T)​I​(x,t−T)−λ​I−D​∂2S∂x2.\begin{array}[]{l}\frac{\partial S}{\partial t}=-SI,\\ \frac{\partial I}{\partial t}=S(x,t-T)\;I(x,t-T)-\lambda I-D\frac{\partial^{2}S}{\partial x^{2}}.\end{array} (18)

This model is similar but not identical to that of Mendez [Mendez 1998]. Consider the wave solution of Eq. (18) with the boundary conditions (15), and studying the stability of the homogeneous solution (S=1,I=0)(S=1,\;I=0), then one gets

(c−Dc)​I′−λ​I+∑n=0(c​T)nn!​dn​Id​zn=0.\left(c-\frac{D}{c}\right)I^{\prime}-\lambda I+\sum_{n=0}\frac{(cT)^{n}}{n!}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{n}I}{\mathrm{d}z^{n}}\;=0.

Substituting with I=em​zI=e^{mz}, then

(c−Dc)​m−λ+exp⁡(c​T​m)=0.\left(c-\frac{D}{c}\right)m-\lambda+\exp(cTm)=0. (19)

Denoting the left hand side of Eq. (19) by f⁡(m)f(m), then it is easy to see that f′​(m)>0​∀c≥Df^{\prime}(m)>0\;\forall\;c\geq\sqrt{D} i.e. f⁡(m)f(m) is monotonically increasing. Furthermore f⁡(0)>0​∀ 0<λ<1.f(0)>0\;\forall\;0<\lambda<1. Thus we have

Proposition 3: The solution (S=1,I=0)(S=1,\;I=0) for Eq. (18) subject to the boundary conditions (15) is asymptotically stable for (z→∞)(z\rightarrow\infty), if the conditions (17) are satisfied.

The derivation of the fraction of survivals σ\sigma after the epidemic wave is similar to the case without delay and is given by Eq. (16).

Also, we will discuss one of the mechanisms of cross diffusion namely recruitment through signals [Saffre and Deneubourg 2002]. In this case swarming individuals e.g. insects recruit others via signals e.g. pheromone for ant colonies. Here we generalize the model of Saffre and Deneubourg to include diffusion, and study the boundedness and persistence of the solutions.

Let uu be the population density and vv be the pheromone density, then

∂u∂t=(α+μ​u)​u​(1−u)−θ​u​v+D1​∂2u∂x2,∂v∂t=θ​u​v−v+D2​∂2v∂x2,\begin{array}[]{c}\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=(\alpha+\mu u)u(1-u)-\theta uv+D_{1}\vskip 12.0pt plus 4.0pt minus 4.0pt\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}},\\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=\theta uv-v+D_{2}\vskip 12.0pt plus 4.0pt minus 4.0pt\frac{\partial^{2}v}{\partial x^{2}},\end{array} (20)

where the parameters α,β,θ,μ\alpha,\beta,\theta,\mu are nonnegative. There are three homogeneous equilibrium solutions

(u,v)=(0,0),(1,0),(1θ,1θ3​(θ−1)​(α​θ+μ)).(u,v)=(0,0),\;(1,0),\;\left(\frac{1}{\theta},\;\frac{1}{\theta^{3}(\theta-1)(\alpha\theta+\mu)}\right).

The solution (0,0)(0,0) is unstable, the solution (1,0)(1,0) is asymptotically stable if θ<1.\theta<1. The third (positive) solution is asymptotically stable if

θ>1,μ(1−2.θ)<α.\theta>1,\;\mu(1-2.\theta)<\alpha.

The results of Cantrell et al [Cantrell et al 1993] are directly applicable to the system (20), hence the solutions of Eq. (20) are persistent if

α>D1​(πL)2,θ>1+D2​(πL)2.\alpha>D_{1}\left(\frac{\pi}{L}\right)^{2},\;\;\;\theta>1+D_{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{L}\right)^{2}. (21)

To study the boundedness of the solutions to Eq. (20), we will consider only solutions satisfying the following condition

u⁡(0)≥0,v⁡(0)≥0⇒u⁡(t)≥0,v⁡(t)≥0​∀t>0.u(0)\geq 0,\;v(0)\geq 0\Rightarrow u(t)\geq 0,\;v(t)\geq 0\;\forall t>0.

It is direct to see that ∂u/∂t<0​∀u>1\partial u/\partial t<0\;\forall\;u>1, hence supu⁡(t)≤1\sup\;u(t)\leq 1. Consequently ∂v/∂t≤(θ−1)​v⇒∀θ≤1\partial v/\partial t\leq(\theta-1)v\;\Rightarrow\;\forall\;\theta\leq 1, then v⁡(t)≤v⁡(0).v(t)\leq v(0). Thus we have:
Proposition 4:

  1. (i)

    For 0≤θ≤10\leq\theta\leq 1, the solutions of the system (20) with D1=D2=0D_{1}=D_{2}=0\;are bounded in R+2={(x,y)​such​that​x≥0,y≥0}R_{+}^{2}=\left\{(x,y)\;\mathrm{such\;that}\;x\geq 0,\;y\geq 0\right\}.

    The solutions of Eq. (20) are persistent given that the conditions (21) are valid.

4 Cross diffusion and evolutionarily stable strategy

Evolutionarily stable strategy ESS [Hofbauer and Sigmund 1998] is an important concept in population dynamics. Consider a population in which each individual adopts one of kk possible strategies. A strategy I∗I^{*} is ESS if for all I≠I∗I\neq I^{*} (yet close to it), then

  1. (i)

    A⁡(I∗,I∗)>A⁡(I,I∗)A(I^{*},I^{*})>A(I,I^{*}); or

  2. (ii)

    If A⁡(I∗,I∗)=A⁡(I,I∗)A(I^{*},I^{*})=A(I,I^{*}), then A⁡(I∗,I)>A⁡(I,I)A(I^{*},I)>A(I,I),

where AA is the payoff matrix. The dynamics of ESS is given by replicator dynamics

d​pid​t=pi[(Ap)i−pAp],i=1,2,3,…,k,\frac{\mathrm{d}p_{i}}{\mathrm{d}t}=p_{i}\left[(Ap)_{i}-pAp\right],\;i=1,2,3,...,k, (22)

where pip_{i} is the fraction of the population adopting the strategy ii.

Recently Hofbauer has introduced the concept of spatial game [Hofbauer 1999], where the system is given by

∂pi∂t=pi​[(A​p)i−p​A​p]+Di​∂2pi∂x2.\frac{\partial p_{i}}{\partial t}=p_{i}\left[(Ap)_{i}-pAp\right]+D_{i}\frac{\partial^{2}p_{i}}{\partial x^{2}}. (23)

This concept is generalized to asymmetric games [Ahmed et al. 2002]. Here we generalize it further to contain cross diffusion in addition to ordinary diffusion. The equations become

∂pi∂t=pi​[(A​p)i−p​A​p]+Di​∂2pi∂x2+∑j≠ikDi​j​∂2pj∂x2.\frac{\partial p_{i}}{\partial t}=p_{i}\left[(Ap)_{i}-pAp\right]+D_{i}\frac{\partial^{2}p_{i}}{\partial x^{2}}+\sum_{j\neq i}^{k}D_{ij}\frac{\partial^{2}p_{j}}{\partial x^{2}}. (24)

The condition ∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}=1 implies Di−Dk+∑j≠ikDi​j=0.D_{i}-D_{k}+\sum_{j\neq i}^{k}D_{ij}=0.

Applying to the hawk(H)-dove(D)- retaliate(R) game [Maynard Smith 1982] where players either fight for a given prize with value vv or agree to share it. The first strategy is called hawk (H) and its drawback is that fight costs value c>vc>v. The second strategy is called dove (D) and its drawback is that it loses against hawks. The third strategy is called retaliate where the player imitates the strategy of the opponent. Hence he (or she) is a hawk (dove) if the opponent is a hawk (dove). Thus the payoff matrix AA is

A=[12​(v−c)v12​(v−c)0v2v212​(v−c)v2v2],A=\left[\begin{array}[]{ccc}\frac{1}{2}(v-c)&v&\frac{1}{2}(v-c)\\ 0&\frac{v}{2}&\frac{v}{2}\\ \frac{1}{2}(v-c)&\frac{v}{2}&\frac{v}{2}\end{array}\right],

where cc and vv are constants and c>v>0c>v>0. Let p1​(p2)p_{1}(p_{2}) be the fraction of population adopting H(D) strategy, respectively, then the system (24) becomes

∂p1∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial p_{1}}{\partial t} =\displaystyle= p1​[−c2+p12​(c−v2)+p2​(v+c)2−p12​c2−c​p1​p2]+\displaystyle p_{1}\left[-\frac{c}{2}+\frac{p_{1}}{2\left(c-\frac{v}{2}\right)}+\frac{p_{2}(v+c)}{2}-\frac{p_{1}^{2}c}{2}-cp_{1}p_{2}\right]+ (25)
D1​∂2p1∂x2+D12​∂2p2∂x2,\displaystyle D_{1}\frac{\partial^{2}p_{1}}{\partial x^{2}}+D_{12}\frac{\partial^{2}p_{2}}{\partial x^{2}},
∂p2∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial p_{2}}{\partial t} =\displaystyle= p2​[p1​(c−v2)−p12​c2−c​p1​p2]+D2​∂2p2∂x2+D21​∂2p1∂x2.\displaystyle p_{2}\left[p_{1}\left(c-\frac{v}{2}\right)-\frac{p_{1}^{2}c}{2}-cp_{1}p_{2}\right]+D_{2}\frac{\partial^{2}p_{2}}{\partial x^{2}}+D_{21}\frac{\partial^{2}p_{1}}{\partial x^{2}}.

Assuming 1≥x≥01\geq x\geq 0, then linear stability analysis shows that p1=p2=0p_{1}=p_{2}=0 is unstable if

D12​D21>D2​(D1+c2​π2).D_{12}D_{21}>D_{2}\left(D_{1}+\frac{c}{2\pi^{2}}\right). (26)

Thus cross diffusion can destabilize equilibrium solution, in some cases, if D12,D21D_{12},D_{21} are large enough.

5 Cross diffusion and the dynamics of learning in multiagent systems

Recently [Sato and Crutchfield 2002] have studied the dynamics of learning in multiagent systems, where the agents use reinforcement learning. They showed that, although the agents are not directly interacting with each other, a collective game between them arises through their interaction with the environment. Such interactions can be modelled via replicator type equations.

Consider two agents uu and vv with nn possible actions, let uj​(t)​(vj​(t))u_{j}(t)\;(v_{j}(t)) be a measure of the probability that the agent u⁡(v)u(v) will take the action jj at time tt. Sato and Crutchfield [Sato and Crutchfield 2002] have shown that uj​(t),vj​(t)u_{j}(t),v_{j}(t) satisfy the following equations

d​uid​t\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}u_{i}}{\mathrm{d}t} =\displaystyle= ui​β1​[(A​v)i−u​A​v]+α1​ui​∑juj​ln⁡(ujui),\displaystyle u_{i}\beta_{1}\left[(Av)_{i}-uAv\right]+\alpha_{1}u_{i}\sum_{j}u_{j}\ln\left(\frac{u_{j}}{u_{i}}\right),
d​vid​t\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}v_{i}}{\mathrm{d}t} =\displaystyle= vi​β2​[(B​u)i−v​B​u]+α2​vi​∑jvj​ln⁡(vjvi),\displaystyle v_{i}\beta_{2}\left[(Bu)_{i}-vBu\right]+\alpha_{2}v_{i}\sum_{j}v_{j}\ln\left(\frac{v_{j}}{v_{i}}\right), (27)

where AA and BB are payoff (reward) matrices for uu and vv, respectively, and α1,α2,β1,β2\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta_{1},\beta_{2} are nonnegative constants. If α1=α2=0\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=0, then one regains the standard asymmetric replicator equations [Hofbauer and Sigmund 1998, Ahmed et al. 2002]. For simplicity we consider the following payoff matrices A=diag⁡(a1,a2),B=diag⁡(b1,b2),ai≥0,bi≥0A=\mathrm{diag}(a_{1},a_{2}),\;B=\mathrm{diag}(b_{1},b_{2}),\;a_{i}\geq 0,\;b_{i}\geq 0, hence the system (27) becomes (u1=u,u2=1−u,v1=v,v2=1−v)(u_{1}=u,\;u_{2}=1-u,\;v_{1}=v,\;v_{2}=1-v)

d​ud​t\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t} =\displaystyle= β1​u​(1−v)​(u⁡(a1+a2)−a2),\displaystyle\beta_{1}u(1-v)\left(u(a_{1}+a_{2})-a_{2}\right),
d​vd​t\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} =\displaystyle= β2​v​(1−u)​(v⁡(b1+b2)−b2).\displaystyle\beta_{2}v(1-u)\left(v(b_{1}+b_{2})-b_{2}\right). (28)

There are four equilibria (u,v)(u,v): E0=(0,0),E1=(a2/(a1+a2),0),E2=(0,b2/(b1+b2)),E3=(1,1)E_{0}=(0,0),\;E_{1}=\left(a_{2}/(a_{1}+a_{2}),0\right),\;E_{2}=\left(0,b_{2}/(b_{1}+b_{2})\right),\;E_{3}=(1,1). The solution E0E_{0} is asymptotically stable while E1,E2,E3E_{1},E_{2},E_{3} are saddle points, hence

Corollary 1: The system (28) is not persistent.

Including cross diffusion the system becomes

u=ue​q+u0​exp⁡(σ​t)​sin⁡π​x,v=ve​q+v0​exp⁡(σ​t)​sin⁡π​x,u=u_{eq}+u_{0}\exp(\sigma t)\sin\pi x,\;v=v_{eq}+v_{0}\exp(\sigma t)\sin\pi x,\;

6 Conclusions

Conditions for Turing instability and persistence in the presence of cross diffusion are derived. The predator-prey model is generalized to the cross diffusion case. Several types of interactions are assumed. .

Stability and persistence of the solutions of an epidemic model with cross diffusion is studied.

The effect of cross diffusion to evolutionary games is studied. In some cases, cross diffusion destabilizes the equilibrium solution.

Conditions for persistence and stability for the dynamics of learning in multiagent systems are concluded.
